item.content: When a filter/guard check compares a value to an empty string (e.g. `x == ""`), consider whether the underlying library may return `None` instead; use truthiness (`not x`) to cover both cases.
Don't trust type annotations from third-party libraries as ground truth—runtime values may violate them (e.g. `str` annotated fields returning `None`). Verify with logs or tests.
When fixing a bug around a specific value, parametrize the existing test over all relevant variants (e.g. `""` and `None`) to lock in the fix and prevent regressions.

When adding new sensor entities to an integration, update all four places consistently: the entity description tuple in sensor.py, icons.json, strings.json (translation names), and the snapshot test file. Missing any one causes test failures or review rejection.

For optional platform data (e.g. load average only present on some OSes), conditionally add entities in async_setup_entry by checking the value is not None, rather than always creating sensors that would stay unknown.
In Home Assistant integrations, secondary/less-common sensors should set entity_registry_enabled_default=False so they are disabled by default, while the primary sensor remains enabled.
When changing a polling/scan interval constant, update the accompanying comment to reflect the new rationale rather than leaving stale justification text that contradicts the new value.

In Home Assistant integrations, the polling interval is set via SCAN_INTERVAL (a timedelta) in const.py; changing it is a one-line edit but the comment explaining the chosen value should be kept accurate.
When a PR proposes changing a timing/interval value, cite upstream evidence (linked issues/PRs, test results from maintainers) in the description to justify the change and preempt reviewer concerns.

When a third-party library changes its data model (e.g. a field replaced by new fields), bump the dependency version in manifest.json AND requirements_all.txt, then update every consumer (sensor/switch update methods) to call the library's refresh method before reading the new fields.

When broadening exception handling (e.g. catching Timeout alongside ConnectionError), parametrize the existing test over each exception type so both paths are covered and the log message is asserted for each.

Don't assume a library's read accessor refreshes data from the server; if the library only updates on explicit calls, call its update/refresh method in the entity's update() before reading state, otherwise sensors show stale values.

When bumping a dependency version, update both manifest.json requirements and requirements_all.txt (and requirements_test_all.txt if the package is used in tests) to the same pinned version; grep the repo for the old version string to catch every occurrence.

Don't assume a dependency bump is purely a version-string change; check the upstream changelog for breaking API changes and update consumers accordingly, but if the changelog shows no relevant API changes, keep the diff minimal to just the version pins.

When migrating a config entry to a new schema (e.g. replacing CONF_LATITUDE/CONF_LONGITUDE with a CONF_LOCATION dict), bump ConfigFlow.VERSION and add async_migrate_entry in __init__.py that moves old keys into the new structure and calls hass.config_entries.async_update_entry(entry, data=..., version=N); update every consumer (setup, unique_id, device_info, config_flow) to read from the new structure.

When switching a config flow to a selector like LocationSelector, use self.add_suggested_values_to_schema(schema, {CONF_LOCATION: {CONF_LATITUDE: ..., CONF_LONGITUDE: ...}}) to prefill defaults from hass.config instead of setting per-field defaults in the schema.

When changing config entry data structure, update the config flow tests and snapshots (e.g. test_config_flow.py, fixtures) to use the new nested data shape; hidden tests will fail if old flat keys remain in test inputs or expected entry data.

When migrating a config flow to LocationSelector, update the strings.json data keys from separate latitude/longitude to a single 'location' key (referencing common::config_flow::data::location) and update the config flow test fixtures/snapshots to the nested {CONF_LOCATION: {CONF_LATITUDE, CONF_LONGITUDE}} shape.

When switching to LocationSelector, don't forget to update the unique_id computation and all consumers (coordinator, setup) that read CONF_LATITUDE/CONF_LONGITUDE directly from entry.data—they must now read from entry.data[CONF_LOCATION].

LocationSelector is configured via LocationSelectorConfig(radius=False) when only lat/long (no radius) is needed; use self.add_suggested_values_to_schema to prefill it from hass.config.latitude/longitude.

For a pure dependency bump, grep the repo for the old version string (e.g. `4.13.3`) to find every pin location (manifest.json, requirements_all.txt, requirements_test_all.txt) and update them all to the same version in one pass.

When bumping a dependency, check the upstream changelog for breaking API changes affecting consumers; if none apply, keep the diff minimal to just the version pins and state in the PR description that tests/mypy pass.

When removing deprecated code, grep the whole integration for every symbol being deleted (e.g. EntityDomainReplacementStrategy, async_finish_entity_domain_replacements) and remove all now-unused imports (including DOMAIN aliases like BINARY_SENSOR_DOMAIN/SENSOR_DOMAIN) from every consumer file, not just the call sites.

Don't leave orphaned helper code behind after removing a deprecation: if a dataclass/function in util.py is only used by the removed deprecation logic, delete it too along with its now-unused imports (dataclass, Iterable, ConfigEntry, HomeAssistant, callback, er, LOGGER).

In Home Assistant, entity deprecation migrations use EntityDomainReplacementStrategy with breaks_in_ha_version; once that HA version has long passed, the replacement strategy and its async_finish_entity_domain_replacements call can be safely deleted from the platform's async_setup_entry.

When fixing type annotations to prepare for a library upgrade (e.g. SQLAlchemy 2.1), align annotations with the actual column/return types (e.g. metadata_id is int not str, nullable columns allow None) and add runtime guards (e.g. skip rows where entity_id is None) where the narrowed type would otherwise be violated.
Don't widen a function parameter type (e.g. Subquery | CompoundSelect) just to satisfy callers; verify what all callers actually pass and narrow the annotation to the real type instead.

In Home Assistant recorder, StatesMeta.metadata_id is an int and StatesMeta.entity_id is nullable; Events columns like context_id and time_fired_ts are nullable, so annotations reading them should allow None.

When a library object is fully mocked in tests, capture the mock (e.g. `with mocked_ec() as mock_ec:`) and assert the exact constructor call arguments (`mock_ec.assert_called_once_with(...)`) so mapping/argument bugs are caught rather than silently passing.
Parametrize tests over a shared list of `pytest.param(..., id=...)` tuples (e.g. LANGUAGE_PARAMS) so multiple tests exercise the same variants consistently and failures are clearly labeled by id.
Place module-level constants (e.g. parametrize parameter lists) before function definitions in test files; reviewers flag constants defined after functions as a readability issue.

When a test asserts a count of listeners/dispatchers/entities that grows as new platforms are added, update both the numeric expectations and the accompanying explanatory comments in the same edit so the comment names every contributing platform.

Don't assume a test failure means the test logic is wrong; when a new platform/feature was added elsewhere, the fix may be to update the expected counts (and comments) in the existing test rather than changing production code.

When removing a deprecated platform (e.g. device_trigger.py), also delete its translation strings in strings.json (device_automation trigger_type entries and the issues/deprecated_* repair strings) and its dedicated test file, and grep for the removed constants (e.g. TOUCH_GESTURE_TRIGGER_MAP, TOUCH_MODELS) to remove now-unused definitions from const.py.

Don't leave orphaned constants or translation keys behind after deleting a deprecated platform: remove the trigger-type map/model constants from const.py if only the deleted module used them, and drop the corresponding strings.json sections so no dangling keys remain.

In Home Assistant, a deprecated device trigger platform is removed by deleting device_trigger.py, its tests, the device_automation trigger_type strings, and the deprecated_device_trigger repair issue strings; the replacement is typically an event entity (e.g. Nanoleaf touch gesture event entity) used with an event.received trigger.

When changing a shared snapshot serializer (e.g. pytest_homeassistant/syrupy.py), grep all .ambr snapshot files for the old placeholder (e.g. `<ANY>`) and regenerate/update every affected snapshot across all integrations, not just the one in the issue example.

In Home Assistant's pytest syrupy serializer, device registry entries are serialized via _serializable_device_registry_entry; via_device_id can be rendered as a device reference using the same _serializable_device_id helper used for other device references, falling back to ANY when the via device cannot be found.
When a snapshot value depends on a config entry id (e.g. wmspro hub identifier built from entry_id), ensure the test uses a fixed entry_id so the new snapshot output is deterministic and stable.

When introducing a StrEnum for state attributes in an input helper integration, define it in const.py, use it in entity.py for both extra_state_attributes and _unrecorded_attributes, and export it from the package __init__.py __all__ next to the existing service enum.
When replacing a constant like ATTR_EDITABLE with a new enum member, remove the now-unused import of the old constant from every consumer file (e.g. entity.py) to avoid lint failures.

In Home Assistant input helper integrations (input_button, input_boolean, etc.), state attributes are exposed via StrEnum classes in const.py (e.g. InputButtonEntityStateAttribute.EDITABLE = 'editable') and exported from the package root alongside the service enum.

For a pure dependency bump where the upstream changelog describes only internal library behavior changes (retry/confirmation logic, serialization) with no API surface changes, keep the diff to just the version pins in manifest.json and requirements_all.txt; do not add workarounds in the integration.
Don't try to compensate in the integration for a bug that the new library version fixes (e.g. stale mode confirmation); the fix belongs upstream, so the HA diff should remain a version bump only.

When replacing string constants with enum members in tests, update the import block too: remove now-unused ATTR_*/SERVICE_* imports and add the enum imports (e.g. ScheduleService, ScheduleEntityStateAttribute, EntityStateAttribute) in the same edit, then grep the test file for each old constant to ensure no leftover references.

Don't assume a test-only refactor to enums is purely mechanical: attribute keys accessed via state.attributes[...] must use the exact enum member (e.g. ScheduleEntityStateAttribute.NEXT_EVENT) matching the production code's enum, and generic attributes like friendly_name/editable/icon use EntityStateAttribute, not the integration-specific enum.

In Home Assistant, integration-specific state/capability attributes are exposed as StrEnums in the integration's const.py (e.g. ScheduleEntityStateAttribute, ScheduleEntityCapabilityAttribute), while generic entity attributes (friendly_name, editable, icon) live in homeassistant.const.EntityStateAttribute; services are exposed as enums like ScheduleService.RELOAD.

When removing unused constants from an integration's const.py, first grep the whole repo for each constant to confirm only tests reference them, then update those tests to use the corresponding enums (service, service argument, entity state/capability attribute) in the same edit so no dangling imports remain.

Don't leave the old string literals (e.g. "set_datetime") in tests after introducing service enums; replace every literal service name and argument key with the enum member (InputDatetimeService.SET, InputDatetimeServiceArgument.DATETIME) so the test exercises the same symbols as production code.

In Home Assistant input helper integrations, service names and service call argument keys are exposed as StrEnums (e.g. InputDatetimeService.SET, InputDatetimeServiceArgument.DATE/TIME/DATETIME/TIMESTAMP) in const.py, so tests should reference these enums rather than raw strings or legacy ATTR_* constants.

When changing a snapshot serializer to conditionally emit a real value instead of a placeholder (e.g. `None if x is None else ANY`), grep all .ambr files for the placeholder and update only the snapshots whose underlying value is actually None; verify by running the affected snapshot tests.

Don't assume a serializer change that replaces a placeholder with a conditional value is safe for all snapshots; check whether the placeholder was masking a real value (e.g. a non-None config_entry_id) that would now be asserted literally and break existing snapshots.

In pytest-home-assistant's syrupy serializer, entity registry entries created directly in the registry (no config entry) have config_entry_id None, while entities set up via snapshot_platform always have a config entry; so `config_entry_id` can be serialized as None when absent and ANY otherwise.

When building a search/catalog over integration descriptions, deduplicate results by domain before applying the result limit: brand aliases (e.g. yalexs_ble listed under both August and Yale) cause the same domain to match multiple sources, so keep the best-ranked match per domain (e.g. via heapq.nsmallest over (rank, name, domain) then dedupe) to avoid returning identical entries twice.

In Home Assistant, async_get_integration_descriptions(hass) returns a dict with 'core' and 'custom' keys, each containing 'integration' and 'helper' sub-dicts; integration entries with 'integration_type' are standalone, while brand entries have an 'integrations' sub-dict mapping domains to metadata. Only entries with config_flow=True can be set up via a config flow.

When adding an LLM Tool to an integration, define name (e.g. 'config__search_integrations'), title, description, annotations (read_only/idempotent/open_world), integration, and a probatio.Schema of parameters, then implement async_call(hass, tool_input, llm_context); resolve the translation language from llm_context.language (falling back to hass.config.language when None or '*') and register the tool in the integration's LLM API tool list.

When adding a new button/entity to an integration that derives entities from a shared list of supported actions (e.g. SUPPORTED_STATION_ACTIONS in const.py), add the new action to that list, add the icon in icons.json and the name in strings.json under the matching translation_key, add the entity to the parametrized test cases, and update any test asserting the total entity count for that device.

Don't forget to bump the expected entity count in test_init.py (e.g. the per-device count parametrize list) when adding a new entity; the snapshot test will regenerate but the explicit count assertion will fail until updated.

In the Ecovacs integration, station action buttons are generated from SUPPORTED_STATION_ACTIONS in const.py; each action (e.g. StationAction.WASH_MOP) needs a translation_key like station_action_wash_mop with entries in strings.json (name) and icons.json (default icon).

When adding a new supported feature to an existing entity (e.g. LawnMowerEntityFeature.STOP), update the supported_features bitmask, implement the corresponding async_<feature> method delegating to the existing command helper, add the service to the parametrized command test cases, and regenerate the snapshot .ambr files whose supported_features integer changes.

Don't forget to update the snapshot .ambr files when a supported_features bitmask changes; the integer value in the snapshot (e.g. <LawnMowerEntityFeature: 7> -> 15) must be regenerated or the snapshot test fails.

In the Ecovacs integration, lawn mower commands are issued via _clean_command(CleanAction.X) (e.g. CleanAction.STOP, PAUSE, START); adding a feature means adding the LawnMowerEntityFeature flag, an async_<feature> override, and a MowerTestCase(CleanV2(CleanAction.X), SERVICE_X) entry in the parametrized test.

When introducing a service StrEnum in an integration (e.g. PersonService in services.py), keep the existing SERVICE_* re-export from the package root intact and use the enum member for the async_register_admin_service call; place the enum definition in services.py (or const.py) and import it in tests from that module.

When removing unused constants from an integration package root (e.g. ATTR_SOURCE, ATTR_DEVICE_TRACKERS), grep the whole repo for each constant first to confirm only tests reference them, then update those tests to use the corresponding enums (integration-specific state attribute enum for integration attributes, EntityStateAttribute for generic ones) in the same edit so no dangling imports remain.

In Home Assistant, the person integration exposes its state attributes via PersonEntityStateAttribute (DEVICE_TRACKERS, EDITABLE, ID, IN_ZONES, USER_ID) in const.py, and its reload action via PersonService.RELOAD in services.py; device tracker attributes used in person tests come from DeviceTrackerEntityStateAttribute, DeviceTrackerEntityCapabilityAttribute, and TrackerEntityStateAttribute.

In Home Assistant, the input_select integration exposes its actions via InputSelectService (SELECT_OPTION, SELECT_NEXT, SELECT_PREVIOUS, SELECT_FIRST, SELECT_LAST, SET_OPTIONS) and service call argument keys via InputSelectServiceArgument (OPTION, OPTIONS) in const.py; the 'options' capability attribute comes from homeassistant.components.select.SelectEntityCapabilityAttribute.OPTIONS, while generic attributes (friendly_name, icon) use homeassistant.const.EntityStateAttribute.

When migrating tests from ATTR_NAME to CONF_NAME for websocket item keys, don't blindly replace every ATTR_* import: ATTR_ENTITY_ID stays as-is (it's a service call argument, not an enum), and the integration's own state attributes (e.g. InputSelectEntityStateAttribute) must be imported from the integration's const.py, not from homeassistant.const.

When converting a test file to use enums, split the import block by source: integration-specific enums (InputSelectService, InputSelectServiceArgument, InputSelectEntityStateAttribute) from the integration's const.py, cross-integration capability enums (SelectEntityCapabilityAttribute) from the base platform module, and generic enums (EntityStateAttribute) plus CONF_NAME from homeassistant.const; keep ATTR_ENTITY_ID as a plain constant.

When adding a new number/entity to an integration, set entity_registry_enabled_default=False for secondary/config entities and include device_class (e.g. NumberDeviceClass.DURATION) plus native_unit_of_measurement (e.g. UnitOfTime.MINUTES) so the entity is properly typed and disabled by default.

When adding a new entity to an integration, don't forget to update the user-facing documentation (e.g. the integration docs page listing supported entities/features); reviewers explicitly request docs updates alongside the code change.

In the Ecovacs integration, number entities are defined as EcovacsNumberEntityDescription entries in number.py with capability_fn (checks caps.settings.<field>), value_fn, key, translation_key, and optional device_class/unit/step; each needs matching entries in icons.json and strings.json under the same translation_key.

When adding a new select entity to the Ecovacs integration, add an EcovacsSelectEntityDescription with capability_fn (caps.settings.<field>), current_option_fn (get_name_key of the event value), options_fn (get_name_key over cap.types), key, translation_key, entity_registry_enabled_default=False and entity_category=EntityCategory.CONFIG, plus matching icons.json and strings.json (name + state map) entries and the snapshot/test updates.

Don't forget to update the user-facing documentation when adding a new entity/feature to an integration; reviewers explicitly request a docs update alongside the code change (this was the sole review comment on the first attempt).

In the Ecovacs integration, select entities are defined as EcovacsSelectEntityDescription entries in select.py; the efficiency mode select uses deebot_client's EfficiencyModeEvent/EfficiencyMode with caps.settings.efficiency_mode and SetEfficiencyMode command, with state keys like standard_mode and energy_efficient_mode.

When refactoring a single-item method to delegate to a batch/list method (e.g. async_execute_command -> async_execute_commands), verify the batch method already performs all side effects (error handling, execution registration, refresh) and move any comments explaining those side effects to the batch method; then confirm the delegation preserves the original default arguments (e.g. refresh_afterwards=True).

Don't submit a PR branch that has fallen behind main and shows a merge conflict; rebase/merge upstream main into the branch and resolve conflicts before requesting review, since a conflicted PR cannot be merged or tested.

In the Overkiz integration, Executor.async_execute_command and async_execute_commands both call coordinator.client.execute_action_group and register the returned exec_id in coordinator.executions keyed by device_url; the action queue can merge concurrent action groups under one exec_id, so registrations must be accumulated (setdefault(...).append(...)) rather than overwritten.

In Home Assistant, aiohttp digest auth rejects ':' in the username (raises ValueError at setup), so test credentials that exercise URL-encoding of special characters should keep ':' out of the username and cover it in the password instead.

When a test fails because a recent change causes a config entry to reload (e.g. credential change triggers reload), trace the failure to the setup path rather than the assertion: the entity may be missing because setup raised, so fix the test input (e.g. an invalid credential) instead of the assertion.

Don't assume a test parametrized over special characters can use any character in any field; check library-level validation (e.g. aiohttp rejecting ':' in usernames) and move the character to a field that accepts it while keeping coverage.

When adding a helper function to a core module (e.g. entity_registry.py), give it a descriptive name that states what it returns/accepts (e.g. `_async_get_child_device_accepting_area`); reviewers frequently flag vague or awkward internal function names even when the logic is correct, so pick a clear name up front.

When a registry update must keep two registries consistent (e.g. moving an entity's area onto its child device), apply the secondary registry update (device_registry.async_update_child_device) before firing the entity registry updated event so listeners never observe an intermediate inconsistent state.

Don't only guard the new behavior on the fields being edited; when a rule depends on the resulting state (e.g. entity has own area but no own name), re-evaluate it after computing the evolved entry and branch on whether the triggering field (e.g. device_id) is among the changed values, so unrelated updates don't accidentally trigger or bypass the logic.

When adding per-device dynamic sensors (e.g. per-disk read/write rates) alongside aggregate sensors, generate the per-device entity descriptions from a helper that returns [] when the device lacks the required data (e.g. io_counters is None), and register a listener that adds sensors for devices that appear later (e.g. a USB drive) by reusing the existing dynamic-listener pattern used for network interfaces.

When a value function needs to look up a specific device by name, wrap it with a decorator (e.g. with_disk) that iterates the device list and returns None if not found, then bind the name via a default argument in the lambda (value=lambda data, k=name: ...) so each generated entity description captures its own device name.

Don't forget to add icons.json entries for every new translation_key, including both the aggregate (disk_read_rate/disk_write_rate) and per-device (disk_device_read_rate/disk_device_write_rate) keys, and add the translation names in strings.json with translation_placeholders for the per-device ones; missing any causes test failures or review rejection.

When a config flow reads a key from an existing entry's data (e.g. reconfigure_entry.data[CONF_PORT]), use .get(key, DEFAULT) for fields that may be absent in legacy entries so reconfiguration of old entries doesn't raise KeyError; add a test that builds a MockConfigEntry without that key and asserts the flow form renders with the default.

Don't assume every config entry has all keys defined in the current schema; entries created before a field was added (e.g. CONF_PORT) will lack it, so direct dict indexing in reconfigure/migration paths crashes—use .get() with the integration's DEFAULT_* constant.
In the Comelit integration, legacy serial-bridge config entries may lack CONF_PORT; DEFAULT_PORT in const.py is the fallback used when prefilling the reconfigure form.

When two pinned dependencies are coupled (e.g. modbus-connection[tmodbus] requires a specific tmodbus version), bump both in the same edit across manifest.json and requirements_all.txt, and state the coupling in the PR description so reviewers understand why both move together.

Don't forget that a dependency may appear as an extra (e.g. modbus-connection[tmodbus]) in one pin and as a standalone package (tmodbus) in another; grep for both the base name and the extra-qualified name to catch every pin location.

In the Home Assistant modbus integration, requirements include pymodbus, modbus-connection[tmodbus], and tmodbus; modbus-connection's tmodbus extra pins a compatible tmodbus version, so the two must be bumped together to matching versions.

For a pure dependency bump where the upstream release notes state the breaking changes are library-internal only (private attributes removed) and the integration already uses the public API, keep the diff to just the version pins in manifest.json and requirements_all.txt; do not touch integration code or tests.

Don't add defensive code or test changes for a dependency bump when the upstream changelog explicitly says the removed APIs were private and the integration already migrated to the public API; the correct diff is version pins only.

When changing how entities are discovered (e.g. from reported sensor values to device metadata/features), update the discovery predicate in every platform that uses it (sensor.py, binary_sensor.py, etc.) and add a coordinator helper (e.g. supported_sensor_keys) that derives the supported keys from the metadata, rather than patching each call site with ad-hoc logic.

Don't forget to populate the test device fixtures' `features` dict when entity creation now depends on it; devices whose fixtures still have `features={}` will produce no entities and fail snapshot/count tests even though the production code is correct.

In the Alexa Devices integration, device metadata is exposed as `features` (a dict of feature type -> instance id -> AmazonDeviceFeature, each with a `sensor_keys` mapping of property -> sensor key), while `sensors` holds the reported values; entity support should be derived from `features` so entities exist before values are reported.

When adding a size/limit guard to a base view class (e.g. max_body_size on HomeAssistantView), apply it in the shared request_handler_factory before the handler runs so it also covers decorators like RequestDataValidator that read the body, and define the limit as a named Final constant in the relevant const.py with a comment explaining the rationale.

When hardening unauthenticated endpoints, don't stop at the obvious auth views: grep for every view with requires_auth = False (onboarding user creation, wait-for-integration, backup restore, etc.) and apply the same limit, since reviewers will ask for the remaining unauthenticated POST bodies to be covered too.

In Home Assistant, the global aiohttp request body limit is 16 MiB (set for Supervisor proxy/ingress/audio-video) and the WebSocket auth message uses aiohttp's 4 MiB default; unauthenticated auth endpoints should be capped far lower (e.g. 64 KiB) since legitimate login/token payloads are only a few KB, returning 413 for oversized bodies.

In the gh-aw quality-scale-reviewer workflow, the API proxy sidecar enforces apiProxy.maxCacheMisses (5) as a single counter shared across all conversations; each parallel subagent starts a fresh conversation (cache miss), so launching 5+ subagents triggers 403 max_cache_misses_exceeded and the Copilot CLI misleadingly reports it as 'Authentication failed with provider'.

When editing a gh-aw workflow, change the source .md file (e.g. .github/workflows/quality-scale-reviewer.md) and let the compiler regenerate the .lock.yml; if you must hand-edit the lock file, update the gh-aw-metadata body_hash to match the new body so the generated file stays consistent.

Don't instruct an agent workflow to fan out parallel subagents for per-item verification when the harness shares a global rate/cache budget; run the checks sequentially in one agent to avoid cache-miss 403s and multiplied credit cost.

When a dependency bump splits a library into new packages (e.g. universal-silabs-flasher 1.2.0 spinning out pygbl and aiospinel), add the new package as an explicit requirement in manifest.json and requirements_all.txt, update imports to the new module, and update tests to patch the new import location.

When a dependency bump moves code into a new package that logs under its own logger name (e.g. aiospinel replacing universal_silabs_flasher.spinel), add the new logger name to the `loggers` list of every integration manifest that listed the old one, otherwise debug logging silently stops showing that traffic.

Don't start a config-flow progress task eagerly (eager_start=True) when the step must return the progress dialog before the task runs; pass eager_start=False to hass.async_create_task so the task doesn't execute synchronously and race the progress step, and move any state it sets (e.g. installing_firmware_name) into the step before creating the task.

When per-device limits/step must come from device-reported capabilities, prefer a dedicated entity subclass that sets the _attr_native_min_value/_attr_native_max_value/_attr_native_step in __init__ from the device model, and select it in async_setup_entry by description.key, rather than adding dynamic properties or per-description static values.

Don't read static device capability values dynamically through properties on every access; reviewers prefer setting them once in the entity constructor (or a subclass) so the values are captured at setup and the entity description stays declarative.

In the La Marzocco integration, the coffee boiler capabilities (target_temperature_min/max/step) are exposed on the CoffeeBoiler model from coordinator.device.dashboard.config[WidgetType.CM_COFFEE_BOILER]; ranges differ per machine (e.g. Linea Micra 80-100°C, GS3 80-110°C) with 0.1°C step.

When a button/entity shows no name because its translation_key has no matching entry in strings.json, grep strings.json for the key used in the platform code and check for a near-miss key (e.g. `resume_all` vs `resume`); rename the existing unused key to the one the code references rather than adding a duplicate, then regenerate the affected snapshot .ambr files since the entity_id and friendly_name change.

Don't assume a missing entity name is a code bug in the platform; check strings.json first—a translation_key mismatch (code uses `resume`, strings.json defines `resume_all`) silently yields an unnamed entity whose entity_id falls back to the device name.

In Home Assistant, an entity's entity_id is derived from its translated name (object_id_base); fixing a missing translation_key changes the entity_id (e.g. button.vm_web -> button.vm_web_resume) and friendly_name, so the snapshot .ambr entries for both the registry entry and state must be regenerated.

In Home Assistant, each integration's quality_scale.yaml lists every quality scale rule under Bronze/Silver/Gold/Platinum tiers with a status of done, todo, or exempt; use exempt only when the rule genuinely does not apply (e.g. docs-triggers when the integration has no triggers) and add a comment explaining the reason for every todo and exempt entry.

When writing a quality_scale.yaml assessment, ground each todo comment in concrete code evidence (file/function names, specific lines like a `== 1` comparison or a missing PARALLEL_UPDATES) and reference the exact rule id it maps to, rather than generic advice; reviewers accept the file when findings are specific and actionable.

Don't mark a quality scale rule as done without checking the actual code: verify config-flow-test-coverage against branch coverage, action-setup against how services resolve the config entry, and unique-config-entry against what the unique ID is derived from, since these are commonly todo even when the integration looks complete.

When a resource (file/connection) is opened lazily on first read and must be closed on early termination, wrap the read callable in a shared helper like ResourceChunkIterator(read, close=..., aclose=...) that handles full-read, error, explicit close, and garbage collection, rather than hand-rolling an __aiter__/__anext__ class.

Don't leave a connection open if it is aborted/closed while still being opened: set a _closed flag, and in the open path use try/finally to call client.abort() when _closed became true during the await, returning None so the caller treats it as end-of-stream.

In Home Assistant, homeassistant.util.async_iterator.ResourceChunkIterator wraps a chunk-reading callable and takes close (sync, e.g. abort) and aclose (async) callbacks, closing the underlying resource on full read, read failure, explicit close, or garbage collection; use it for backup download streams instead of custom iterator classes.

When removing a deprecated compatibility shim (e.g. a deprecated effect/state mapping), remove all four artifacts in one pass: the mapping constant and its branch in the platform code, the now-unused imports it required (issue_registry helpers, DOMAIN), the repair-issue translation block in strings.json, and the dedicated test that covered the shim.

Don't leave the repair-issue strings.json block behind after deleting the async_create_issue call that referenced it; grep strings.json for the translation_key (e.g. deprecated_effect_none) and remove the whole issues entry, since dangling translation keys fail hassfest/translation checks.

Don't forget to prune imports that only the removed deprecation logic used (e.g. IssueSeverity, async_create_issue, DOMAIN, ATTR_EFFECT, LIGHT_DOMAIN, SERVICE_TURN_ON, issue_registry) from both the platform module and the test file; ruff will flag them and reviewers expect a clean diff.

When promoting an integration's quality scale tier (e.g. to bronze), set "quality_scale": "<tier>" in manifest.json AND remove the integration's domain from the corresponding exclusion list in script/hassfest/quality_scale.py (e.g. the bronze exclusion set); both edits are required or hassfest validation fails.

Don't leave a config-flow test ending on an abort result when the test is meant to exercise a form error path; continue the flow after the error to reach a success result, since abort is only a valid terminal result for tests that intentionally abort.

In Home Assistant, script/hassfest/quality_scale.py maintains per-tier exclusion lists of integration domains that do not yet meet a tier; an integration is considered to have a tier only when its manifest quality_scale field is set and its domain is absent from that tier's exclusion list.

When bumping an integration's quality scale tier, verify every rule in the target tier (and all lower tiers) in quality_scale.yaml is marked done or exempt before editing the manifest; the manifest change alone is metadata-only and hassfest validates consistency.

candidate.content: Don't bump the manifest quality_scale field without also removing the integration's domain from the corresponding tier exclusion list in script/hassfest/quality_scale.py; both edits are required or hassfest validation fails.

item.content: In Home Assistant, a quality scale tier bump is a metadata-only change (manifest.json quality_scale field plus the hassfest exclusion list); it requires no runtime code changes and is validated by hassfest, so keep the diff minimal.

When adding a sensor that only some device models support, add an exists_fn predicate (defaulting to lambda _: True) to the entity description dataclass and filter descriptions in async_setup_entry with `if description.exists_fn(coordinator.data)`, rather than always creating the entity and leaving it unknown.

Don't rely solely on an exists_fn that reads a live value (e.g. humidity > 0) to decide entity creation: exists_fn runs only at setup, so a transient property-read error (library maps BACnet errors to 0) can permanently suppress the entity until reload. Consider a follow-up test for the initial-read-error case and note the limitation.

In the Flexit Nordic (BACnet) integration, flexit_bacnet exposes extract_air_humidity (BACnet AI96, relative humidity in %) only on models with a built-in humidity sensor; other models report 0, so the sensor should be gated on the value being > 0.

In Home Assistant's DataUpdateCoordinator, UpdateFailed(retry_after=N) REPLACES the configured update interval rather than extending it, so a hub with a long interval (e.g. Overkiz UPDATE_INTERVAL_ALL_ASSUMED_STATE = 60 min) will poll every retry_after seconds while rate limited; floor retry_after at the coordinator's default update interval (max(RATE_LIMIT_RETRY_AFTER, self._default_update_interval)) so backoff never speeds polling up.

When fixing a backoff/retry interval that must not shorten a longer configured interval, write a test that ticks the full configured interval, then asserts no fetch occurs at the shorter retry_after and exactly one fetch occurs at the configured interval; this proves the floor without relying on internal coordinator state.

Don't assume a retry_after/backoff value only delays the next poll; in HA's DataUpdateCoordinator it overrides the update interval entirely, so a value shorter than the configured interval makes the integration poll faster during an error condition—always compare retry_after against the configured interval.

When gating behavior on host hardware (e.g. total memory via os.sysconf('SC_PAGE_SIZE') * os.sysconf('SC_PHYS_PAGES')), define the threshold as a named constant with a comment explaining why it differs from the documented minimum (e.g. Raspberry Pi reserves memory for the GPU), and add an autouse fixture that patches the helper to a generous default so existing tests are unaffected, plus a dedicated test for the helper itself.

Don't add a new hardware/environment check to a config-flow branch without an autouse test fixture that mocks it to the permissive default; otherwise every existing test that exercises that branch (e.g. zeroconf onboarding) will start failing on CI machines whose real value falls below the threshold.

In Home Assistant, os.sysconf('SC_PAGE_SIZE') * os.sysconf('SC_PHYS_PAGES') returns the host's physical memory in bytes from inside the Core container; a Raspberry Pi reports less than its nominal RAM (e.g. ~903 MB visible on a 1 GB Pi 3), so memory thresholds should be set below the documented minimum (e.g. 1.5 GB for the 2 GB Matter Server requirement).

When wrapping a third-party client exception in HomeAssistantError, raise it with `from err` and assert `exc_info.value.__cause__ is <the original error>` in the test so the cause chain is locked in, not just the message.

When a failure can surface through multiple entry points (direct helper call, HTTP proxy endpoint, service action), parametrize a fixture over the failing client method (e.g. streams.list, streams.add, get_jpeg_snapshot) and write one test per entry point that reuses that fixture, so every request path and every underlying failure is covered.

Don't assert only that an error is raised for a camera snapshot failure; also assert the side effects did not happen (snapshot file not written, stream not started) and that the HTTP proxy returns 500 without logging 'Error handling request', since an unhandled exception would otherwise leak into the logs.

Don't leave translation strings in Title Case when the surrounding entries use sentence case; reviewers (and Lokalise post-merge) flag inconsistent casing. Match the existing style: device_automation trigger_subtype entries are Title Case ('Hold Press') while entity state names are sentence case ('Hold press').

When adding a new event/state variant to an integration that exposes it in multiple places, update all of them in one pass: the event entity's event_types tuple, the device_trigger trigger subtype set, strings.json (trigger_subtype name, entity state name, and any [%key:...%] alias), the dependency bump in manifest.json + requirements_all.txt, and the parametrized test cases in both test_event.py and test_device_trigger.py.

In the BTHome integration, button event types are listed in event.py (BTHomeEventEntityDescription event_types) and device_trigger.py (EVENT_CLASS_BUTTON subtype set); each event type needs a strings.json entry under both device_automation.trigger_subtype and entity.event.button.state_attributes.event_type.state, and the bthome-ble library must be bumped to a version that parses the new event id (e.g. 0x81 hold_release in 3.25.0) or the event entity raises ValueError.

Don't reuse a generic action translation (e.g. 'start': 'Starting' borrowed from a common action) for a state value in a new entity's state map; each state needs its own semantically correct label (e.g. 'start': 'Starting' for an emergency-charge control state, not a shared action string), since reviewers flag wrong translations even when the key exists.

When a dependency bump's changelog adds new topics/entities, update strings.json for every new entity: add the entity name under entity.<platform>.<key>.name and, for enum/state entities, a state map with a distinct label per state value; then verify the labels read correctly in context rather than copying from a similar existing entry.

In the victron_gx integration, entity translations live in strings.json under entity.<platform>.<translation_key> with a 'name' and optional 'state' map; new victron-mqtt topics surface as new entity keys (e.g. alternator_emergency_charge_control, alternator_emergency_charge_blocked_countdown) that must be added there when bumping the library.

When sentence-casing translation strings, apply the change only to the specific section flagged (e.g. device_automation.trigger_subtype) and leave single-word entries (Off, On, Press, Toggle) untouched; multi-word entries get only the first word capitalized.

Don't assume a casing fix requires code or snapshot changes; strings.json edits alone don't alter entity_ids or snapshots when the changed keys are device_automation trigger_subtype labels, so keep the diff to strings.json.

In Home Assistant string style, device_automation trigger_subtype labels follow sentence case (e.g. 'Double press', 'Rotate left'), while entity state names are also sentence case; only proper nouns and the first word are capitalized.

When adding a cache keyed on an object identity that may be mutated in place (e.g. a bytearray payload), skip caching for those types and add a dedicated test that mutates the object in place and asserts the cache is bypassed (e.g. test_value_template_bytearray_changed_in_place).

When adding an optional keyword-only parameter to a widely used helper (e.g. value_json on Template.async_render_with_possible_json_value), use a sentinel default (e.g. _SENTINEL) so callers that don't pass it keep the old parse behavior, and pass UNDEFINED explicitly to mean 'already parsed, not JSON'.

Don't cache a parse result keyed on a mutable payload object without checking its type; bytearray (and similar) can change in place between subscribers, so the cache must be skipped for those types or it will return stale JSON.

Don't strip or rewrite the PR template when submitting; keep the full template and tick the relevant Type of change and Checklist boxes (e.g. 'I understand the code I am submitting and can explain how it works'), since reviewers reject otherwise-correct dependency bumps solely for a missing/edited template.

When a dependency bump fixes a bug in the library (e.g. wrong sign on a negative temperature, returning None instead of a false negative), describe the upstream fix in the PR description but keep the HA diff to the version pins unless the integration code must adapt to the new return type (e.g. handling None).

In the electrasmart integration, the dependency is pyElectra pinned in manifest.json requirements and requirements_all.txt; the package name is case-sensitive (pyElectra), so grep for the exact string when bumping.

When adding a code owner to an integration, update both CODEOWNERS (add /homeassistant/components/<domain>/ and /tests/components/<domain>/ lines with the @handle, keeping alphabetical order) and the integration's manifest.json codeowners list; both are required for the change to be complete.
Don't forget to add the tests directory entry (/tests/components/<domain>/) to CODEOWNERS when claiming ownership of an integration; adding only the component path leaves test ownership unassigned.

In Home Assistant, integration ownership is declared in two places: the CODEOWNERS file (component and tests paths) and the integration's manifest.json "codeowners" array (GitHub handles prefixed with @); an integration with an empty codeowners list has no owner.

When adding a new platform (e.g. light) to an integration that already has other platforms, mirror the existing platform's async_setup_entry pattern: track known_devices, register a coordinator listener that adds entities for newly discovered devices, and gate entity creation on a device metadata predicate (e.g. primary_display_category == 'LIGHT') rather than on reported sensor values.

Don't derive device capabilities (e.g. supported light modes/effects) from ad-hoc feature lookups when the device metadata already exposes them (e.g. features['mode'] with modeOptions, or a supported_modes field); reviewers will ask you to use the resolved metadata instead of re-parsing raw configuration.

Don't wrap API calls in a bare try/except without passing the coordinator to the shared error-handling helper (e.g. alexa_api_call(coordinator)); the coordinator is what captures/logs errors, so omitting it silently swallows failures and reviewers flag it.

When removing a deprecated API method that is called across many integrations (e.g. ConfigFlow._set_confirm_only), grep the whole repo for every call site and remove them all in one pass, then turn the method into a no-op that reports usage (raising for core integrations, ignoring for custom) so the call cannot be reintroduced; also remove the corresponding key from the context TypedDict.

Don't leave the removed API's context key or helper in place after dropping its call sites: when deleting a flag like confirm_only, remove the key from the ConfigFlowContext TypedDict and any tests asserting it, not just the _set_confirm_only() calls in each config flow.

In Home Assistant, ConfigFlow._set_confirm_only() set a confirm_only flag in the flow context for a frontend feature that was never built; nothing in core or the frontend ever consumed it, so it is safe to remove from all config flows and from ConfigFlowContext.

When deprecating YAML import for an integration, add async_create_issue in async_setup (guarded by `if DOMAIN not in config: return True`) with domain=HOMEASSISTANT_DOMAIN, issue_id=f"deprecated_yaml_{DOMAIN}", breaks_in_ha_version, is_fixable=False, issue_domain=DOMAIN, severity=IssueSeverity.WARNING, translation_key="deprecated_yaml", and translation_placeholders with domain and integration_title; the deprecated_yaml translation already exists in homeassistant strings so no new strings.json entry is needed.

When adding a YAML-import deprecation test, patch the integration's feed manager update method (e.g. aio_geojson_geonetnz_quakes.GeonetnzQuakesFeedManager.update) to avoid network calls, call async_setup_component with a full YAML config dict, await hass.async_block_till_done(), then assert issue_registry.async_get_issue(domain=HOMEASSISTANT_DOMAIN, issue_id=f"deprecated_yaml_{DOMAIN}") is not None.

In Home Assistant, YAML-import deprecation issues are created under HOMEASSISTANT_DOMAIN (homeassistant.core.DOMAIN) with issue_id f"deprecated_yaml_{DOMAIN}" and translation_key "deprecated_yaml"; the translation_placeholders must include both "domain" and "integration_title" (the human-readable integration name).

When a pairing/validation loop waits for a field that some device firmware omits (e.g. 'name' in initial MQTT telemetry), wait only on the condition that is universally present (e.g. non-empty reported state) and apply a fallback default for the optional field afterwards, rather than looping until the optional field appears.

Don't capture a mutable state dictionary (e.g. roomba_reported_state(roomba)) in __init__ and read it from entity properties; the library replaces the dict on each message, so entities go stale. Expose it as a @property that re-queries the library each access, and add a test that replaces the dict instance after setup and asserts the state updates.

Don't pass a possibly-None value into DeviceInfo name/model; when a device may omit its name, coerce with str(...) or a fallback (e.g. .get('name') or 'Roomba') so the device and its entities are never named 'None'.

Don't write tests that assert on internal implementation details (e.g. directly calling a value_fn or checking a private helper's return); reviewers reject them as 'testing an internal'. Test through the public entity state (hass.states.get(...).state) or the snapshot instead.

When adding a binary_sensor platform to an integration, add Platform.BINARY_SENSOR to the PLATFORMS list in __init__.py, create binary_sensor.py with a frozen dataclass entity description carrying a value_fn, add strings.json entity.binary_sensor.<key>.name entries, and add a snapshot test file under tests/components/<domain>/snapshots/.

In Home Assistant, connectivity binary sensors (device_class=CONNECTIVITY) that merely reflect whether the device is reachable should be marked entity_category=EntityCategory.DIAGNOSTIC and entity_registry_enabled_default=False, since they are noise for most users.

When writing init/setup tests for an integration, parametrize a single test over all error scenarios (library API errors, ClientError, TimeoutError, HTTP 4xx/5xx) with pytest.param(..., id=...) tuples asserting both the resulting ConfigEntryState and the triggered flow sources (e.g. SOURCE_REAUTH for auth errors), rather than writing one test per scenario; reviewers explicitly prefer one grouped parametrized test.

Don't write separate near-identical tests for each setup failure mode (API error, bad request, client error, timeout, HTTP error, auth error); reviewers will ask you to merge them into one parametrized test covering all scenarios with expected state and flow sources as parameters.

In the Pterodactyl integration, setup failures map to ConfigEntryState.SETUP_RETRY for PterodactylApiError/BadRequestError/ClientError/TimeoutError/HTTP 5xx, while a 401 ClientResponseError triggers ConfigEntryState.SETUP_ERROR and starts a SOURCE_REAUTH flow; tests mock mock_pterodactyl.client.servers.list_servers.side_effect to inject the error.

Don't include 'unknown' as a value in a SensorDeviceClass.ENUM sensor's options list; map the unknown/None state to None in the value function and exclude it from options (e.g. `[s.value for s in State if s is not State.UNKNOWN]`), since reviewers reject 'unknown' as an option.

When adding per-item dynamic sensors (e.g. one level+state sensor per battery), generate the entity descriptions from a helper that takes the item and returns its descriptions, bind the item key via a default argument in the lambda (`value=lambda data, k=name: ...`), and register a coordinator listener that adds sensors for items appearing after setup; set entity_registry_enabled_default based on whether the item is already covered by aggregate sensors (e.g. disabled for the system's own battery, enabled for peripheral devices).

In the System Bridge integration, systembridgeconnector exposes battery data via data.battery (state, power, voltage, ac_connected, batteries list of BatteryInfo with name/model/scope/percentage/state); BatteryScope.DEVICE marks peripheral batteries (mouse/headset) while the system's own battery is covered by the main battery sensors, and ac_connected is None on desktops with no mains supply.

When moving entities from a shared/coordinator device to a new per-item device (e.g. ZHA group devices), preserve entity identity by keeping the existing unique_id and entity_id: derive the new device identifier from the config entry id plus a stable item key, and migrate custom names/areas from the old device to the new one so automations keep working.

When introducing a new device type into an integration, audit every device-scoped code path that assumes a real hardware device (device_trigger, diagnostics, device_info, entity naming) and add an early branch for the new device kind (e.g. return [] for triggers, return group_info for diagnostics) rather than letting it fall through to hardware-only logic.

Don't create a per-item device unconditionally; tie its lifecycle to the entities it owns (create when the item has entities, remove when it drops below the threshold or is deleted) and restore the device and entities from the registries' deleted entries when the item reappears, so stale devices don't accumulate.

When making an integration's exceptions translatable (quality scale rule exception-translations), raise with translation_domain=DOMAIN, translation_key=<key>, and translation_placeholders={...} instead of a hardcoded string, keep `from err` chaining so the raw error stays in logs, add an "exceptions" block in strings.json with a "message" per key, and flip the rule to done in quality_scale.yaml.

Don't include the raw underlying exception text in the translated message string itself; pass it via translation_placeholders (e.g. {error}) so the message stays a plain translatable sentence while the detail is still shown.

In Home Assistant, exception translations live in strings.json under an "exceptions" key, each entry having a "message" field; the raised exception references them via translation_domain/translation_key/translation_placeholders (e.g. UpdateFailed(translation_domain=DOMAIN, translation_key="update_error", translation_placeholders={"error": str(err)})).

Don't hardcode fixed values like ports (e.g. ':8088') into translatable exception message strings; pass them as translation_placeholders instead, since translators shouldn't translate IP/port literals and a future port change would invalidate existing translations.

When making an integration's exceptions translatable, grep the integration for every hardcoded error string (ConfigEntryNotReady, HomeAssistantError, UpdateFailed) and convert each to translation_domain/translation_key/translation_placeholders, then add a matching 'exceptions' block in strings.json with one 'message' per key.

In the Logitech Harmony Hub integration, connection failures in data.py raise ConfigEntryNotReady with the hub name and address; the address is a config value and the port 8088 is fixed, so both should be passed as translation_placeholders rather than embedded in the message text.

When adding a reconfigure flow, extract the shared location/option handling into a helper (e.g. _async_handle_location(step_id, data_schema, location_type, api_key)) called by both async_step_user and async_step_reconfigure, and prefill the sub-steps (coordinates/country) from self._get_reconfigure_entry().data when self.source == SOURCE_RECONFIGURE, falling back to hass.config defaults otherwise.

When adding a reconfigure flow that changes the location type, don't merge the new data into the old entry data; use async_update_reload_and_abort(entry, data_updates=...) or replace the data entirely so keys from the previous location type (CONF_COUNTRY_CODE vs CONF_LATITUDE/CONF_LONGITUDE) are dropped, and leave the entry title unchanged.

In the Electricity Maps (co2signal) integration, the config flow stores either CONF_COUNTRY_CODE or CONF_LATITUDE/CONF_LONGITUDE depending on the chosen location type (TYPE_USE_HOME, TYPE_SPECIFY_COORDINATES, TYPE_SPECIFY_COUNTRY); the API key is handled by reauth, so a reconfigure flow should only change the location and mark the reconfiguration-flow quality scale rule done.

In Home Assistant, timestamps loaded from storage via parse_datetime carry a fixed UTC offset (the offset in effect when written), not the configured time zone; anything that computes wall-clock times from them (e.g. CronSim seeding for the backup schedule) must convert with dt_util.as_local first, otherwise schedules drift by an hour after a DST change until restart.

When fixing a DST/timezone bug, write a parametrized test covering both DST directions (summer->winter and winter->summer) with a stored timestamp carrying the old offset, asserting both the reported next-run time (with the new offset) and that the scheduled action fires at the configured local time and not an hour early/late.

Don't assume a timezone/DST fix must also rewrite the stored timestamp; if the stored value is only used as a seed and the consumer converts it to local time, keep the fix at the consumption point and explain in the PR why the stored value does not need changing (reviewers will ask where else the value is used).

When moving entities onto per-channel/per-item child devices, keep the existing unique_id and entity_id so history and automations survive, and migrate custom names/areas from the old device; then regenerate the affected snapshot .ambr files since friendly_name and device references change.

When replacing indexed translation keys (e.g. indexed_current with translation_placeholders={'index': '1'}) with per-channel entities, rename the translation key to the unindexed form (current) and drop the placeholders, since the channel is now conveyed by the child device name; update strings.json and icons.json accordingly.

Don't create per-channel entities unconditionally; gate them on a channel_condition predicate that checks the device actually reports the second channel (e.g. DPCode.CUR_POWER2 in device.status_range) so single-channel devices don't get phantom entities.

In Home Assistant, an entity registry entry's `next_name_part` (NextNamePart enum from homeassistant.helpers.registry) indicates which name component the entity contributes: NextNamePart.DEVICE means the entity has no name of its own and inherits the device name, so `entry.entity_name` is empty for it.

When adding a keyword-only flag to a template function (e.g. `fallback` on entity_name), register it in the TemplateFunction's parameters list with a default so the positional form still works, and add tests for both the positional call and the filter form (`'{{ x | entity_name(fallback=True) }}'`).

When a template helper should fall back to a related registry object's name (e.g. device name when the entity has no own name), resolve it via the device registry (`dr.async_get(hass).async_get(device_id)`) and prefer `name_by_user or name`; gate the fallback on the entity actually inheriting that name (next_name_part) rather than on the name merely being empty.

When adding a backup agent to an integration, implement backup.py with async_get_backup_agents (one agent per enabled subentry), async_register_backup_agents_listener (store listeners in hass.data under a DATA_BACKUP_AGENT_LISTENERS key), and a BackupAgent subclass; in __init__.py register entry.async_on_state_change to notify those listeners so the backup integration refreshes its agent list when entries load/unload.

When uploading large files through a proxy-limited API, split the upload into fixed-size chunks (e.g. 50 MiB, below Cloudflare's 100 MB body limit) and report progress via the OnProgressCallback; stream downloads rather than buffering the whole file, and wrap all client calls in a decorator that converts library errors (timeout vs generic) into BackupAgentError with translation_domain/translation_key.

Don't re-list the remote directory on every download/delete lookup when the listing downloads every metadata file; cache the parsed listing with a short TTL (e.g. 300s) and invalidate it on upload/delete, so repeated backup operations don't hammer the API.

When a passive Bluetooth integration's entities should become unavailable after the device stops advertising, remove any `available`/`assumed_state` overrides that force True and let the PassiveBluetoothProcessorCoordinator's availability flow through; if the Silver log-when-unavailable rule must be met, subclass the coordinator and override _async_handle_unavailable / _async_handle_bluetooth_event with a logged-once flag, then update the quality_scale.yaml comments to describe the actual behavior.

Don't leave a quality_scale.yaml rule marked done with a comment that contradicts the code (e.g. claiming assumed_state is used when entities now go unavailable); update the comment text in the same edit so the documented rationale matches the implementation.

Don't merge a behavior change that invalidates existing user-facing documentation without opening and linking the docs follow-up PR in the description; reviewers block otherwise-correct changes until the docs update is tracked.

When introducing a state-attribute StrEnum for an integration, also replace string literals used in state.attributes.get(...) lookups (e.g. restore-state reads in async_added_to_hass) and in test assertions with the enum members, and remove the now-unused ATTR_* imports from both the platform module and tests in the same edit.

Don't blindly rename an existing attribute constant to a new enum member name when the underlying string value is user-visible (e.g. ATTR_CUR = 'cur' -> 'current'); changing the string changes the state attribute key and breaks existing automations/templates, so keep the original string value unless the PR explicitly intends a breaking change.

In Home Assistant, the script integration's state attributes (last_triggered, mode, current, max, last_action) are exposed via ScriptEntityStateAttribute in homeassistant/components/script/const.py, mirroring AutomationEntityStateAttribute; ATTR_LAST_TRIGGERED is kept for custom integrations that import it, while ATTR_LAST_ACTION is unused and can be removed.

When adding diagnostics.py to a Bluetooth integration, build the diagnostics dict from the coordinator status plus bluetooth.async_last_service_info(hass, address, connectable=False), and re-parse the advertisement with the library's device-data class (e.g. OralBBluetoothDeviceData().update(service_info)) to expose model/manufacturer/versions and sensor/binary_sensor values; return early with None fields when no advertisement has been seen.

Don't put a runtime `assert address is not None` in diagnostics code; reviewers require the narrowing assert to be inside `if TYPE_CHECKING:` (importing TYPE_CHECKING from typing) so it is not executed at runtime.

In Home Assistant diagnostics for Bluetooth integrations, the config entry unique_id is the device MAC address; since device names/titles embed part of the MAC, omit the address, unique_id, config entry id and device name from the diagnostics and expose only model/manufacturer/version and parsed sensor values.
